The repo does not contain the official deadline or upload instructions. Confirm today in the challenge Discord:

- Exact cutoff time and timezone
- Upload portal and accepted format/size
- Whether a ZIP, repository link, or both are required
- Whether a final held-out chunk has been released
- Presentation/demo logistics

## Required submission package

Create one `submission/` folder containing:

- `SUBMISSION.md`
- `router/` — runnable source code
- `results/`
  - `routes.jsonl`
  - cost–quality frontier CSV and PNG
  - judge-model scores, if used
  - public/fit and held-out results clearly separated
- `presentation.html` or an exported PDF

`SUBMISSION.md` must state:

- Team name and members
- Objective and chosen trade-off
- Nameable routing signal
- Held-out, cache-aware headline result
- Off-policy evaluation method
- Weakest known failure mode
- Exact clean-checkout reproduction commands

## Evaluation requirements

The solution should demonstrate:

- A cost–quality frontier, not merely one operating point
- Honest off-policy evaluation
- Cache-aware pricing
- No refitting on the held-out evaluation split
- Estimated tokens explicitly labeled as estimates
- Pricing explicitly labeled as an assumption
- Selection bias and other failure modes disclosed
- Every headline number reproducible from committed scripts

## Five-minute presentation

The judged defense requires:

- One chart: the cost–quality frontier
- One clear claim
- One genuine weakness
- Headline result from the held-out split
- Explanation of the routing signal and off-policy method
- Every displayed number traceable to reproducible output

## Legal and packaging checks

- Never include `export/`, `export_linked/`, archives, or raw trajectories.
- Keep the repository private.
- Test reproduction from a clean checkout.
- Scan the package for leaked trajectory text.
- ZIP the `submission/` directory.
- Generate and submit its SHA-256 checksum.

content.text:
The repo is best understood as a three-stage system:

```text
Opening request → predict required tier → T1/T2/T3
Full trajectory → infer observed difficulty → D1/D2/D3
Then compare tier against difficulty and estimated cost
```

It does not directly measure answer correctness, and it does not yet act as a live API gateway. It estimates whether an abstract model tier would be sufficient.

## 1. What the evaluator quantifies

Because the export has no final outputs or quality labels, the evaluator treats observed agent effort as a proxy for task difficulty.

From the deepest request in each reconstructed trajectory, it counts:

| Effort metric | Weight |
|---|---:|
| Tool calls | 22% |
| LLM responses | 18% |
| Generated tokens | 16% |
| Context tokens | 10% |
| Tool errors | 10% |
| Distinct tools used | 8% |
| Tool-output tokens | 6% |
| Maximum same-tool retry streak | 4% |
| User turns | 3% |
| Reasoning tokens | 3% |

Implementation: [difficulty.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/evaluator/difficulty.py:28), extraction: [metrics.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/evaluator/metrics.py:68).

Each metric is converted to a right-ECDF percentile rank:

\[
r_k(i)=\frac{\#\{j:x_{jk}\le x_{ik}\}}{N}
\]

The evaluator score is:

\[
E_i=\sum_k w_k r_k(i)
\]

The weights sum to one. The score is then cut at its 55th and 85th percentiles:

- Bottom 55% → D1
- Next 30% → D2
- Top 15% → D3

Two hard overrides force D3:

- At least five detected tool errors
- At least 40 tool calls

Thus “difficulty” really means high observed effort, not necessarily intrinsic difficulty or semantic answer quality.

## 2. What the router sees

The router sees only information available before execution:

- System prompt
- First user message
- Tool definitions

It cannot see:

- Later tool calls
- Tool failures
- Assistant responses
- Evaluator metrics
- Logged model identity

Feature extraction is in [features.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/router/features.py:76).

### Hand-built heuristic

Features are percentile-ranked, averaged within four groups, then combined:

| Group | Sign | Group weight | Meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Ask | + | 1.5 | Entities, questions, actions, coordination, URLs, length, attachments |
| Harness | + | 0.7 | System complexity, skills, flags, subagent support |
| Breadth | − | 0.8 | Number/size of generic tools |
| Mid-thread | − | 0.8 | Existing context, activity triggers, auto-read blocks |

The exact formula is:

\[
H_i=\frac{
1.5\,ask_i+0.7\,harness_i-0.8\,breadth_i-0.8\,midthread_i
}{3.8}
\]

It is min-max normalized afterward. Features within each group have equal weight before the group weight is applied. See [tiering.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/router/tiering.py:22).

The negative signs encode the empirical claim that broad generic tool environments and mid-thread requests often correspond to small remaining workloads.

### Learned router

The learned model combines:

- Word TF-IDF: 1–2 grams
- Character TF-IDF: 3–5 grams
- Numeric routing features, percentile-ranked

It fits two cumulative logistic classifiers:

\[
P(D\ge2),\qquad P(D\ge3)
\]

These are converted into:

- \(P(D\le1)\)
- \(P(D\le2)\)
- Class probabilities for D1/D2/D3

Predictions are out-of-fold using five-fold `GroupKFold`, grouping tasks by workspace fingerprint. This prevents the model from memorizing workspace-specific request patterns. See [ml.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/router/ml.py:95).

## 3. How a tier is selected

The repo supports several dispatch rules.

### Default: 85/15 blend

The ML difficulty score is:

\[
M_i=1-\frac{P(D\le1)+P(D\le2)}{2}
\]

The default router score is:

\[
R_i=0.85\,rank(M_i)+0.15\,rank(H_i)
\]

It then assigns:

- Bottom 55% → T1
- Next 30% → T2
- Top 15% → T3

The defaults are defined in [run_pipeline.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/run_pipeline.py:67).

### Quality-safe τ router

With the default \(\tau=0.80\):

```text
If P(D≤1) ≥ 0.80 → T1
else if P(D≤2) ≥ 0.80 → T2
else → T3
```

This intentionally over-routes uncertain tasks. Its reported operating point is:

- 94.7% served
- 89.4% cost-weighted served
- 72.5% of the all-T3 cost

### Cost-aware λ router

For each task and tier, it minimizes:

\[
\widehat C_i(t)+\lambda P(D_i>t)
\]

Here:

- \(\widehat C_i(t)\) is predicted cost at routing time
- \(P(D_i>t)\) is the probability that tier \(t\) is insufficient
- Default \(\lambda=0.3\)

The cost predictor estimates context tokens, generated tokens, and LLM-call count using routing-time features. Using realized trajectory cost instead would be an oracle and is reported separately.

## 4. What “served” means

A task is considered served when:

\[
T_i\ge D_i
\]

Examples:

- T1 for D1: served
- T2 for D1: served but over-routed
- T2 for D3: not served
- T3 for any difficulty: served

This is a binary sufficiency assumption—not a measured counterfactual outcome.

The repo supports it with a split-half natural-experiment check: on matched hard tasks, lower-tier models showed:

- +6.7 percentage points tool-error rate
- +2.7 additional retry streak
- Both bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero

That is evidence that under-routing has consequences, but it still does not prove answer correctness.

## 5. Cost and weighted quality

For task \(i\) at tier \(t\):

\[
C_{it}=
\frac{
T_i p^{input}_t+
T_i\frac{n_i-1}{2}p^{cached}_t+
g_i p^{output}_t
}{10^6}
\]

Where:

- \(T_i\): estimated context tokens
- \(g_i\): recovered generated tokens
- \(n_i\): estimated LLM responses
- All token counts use characters/4
- The replay term approximates cached prefix growth

Assumed prices per million tokens are:

| Tier | Input | Cached input | Output |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| T1 | $0.20 | $0.02 | $1.20 |
| T2 | $2.00 | $0.20 | $10.00 |
| T3 | $5.00 | $0.50 | $25.00 |

These are assumptions because model IDs are anonymized. See [run_pipeline.py](C:/Users/marks/Documents/entire-viktor-tumai-ehk/run_pipeline.py:62).

There are two served metrics:

\[
served=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\mathbf1[T_i\ge D_i]
\]

\[
weighted\ served=
\frac{\sum_i\mathbf1[T_i\ge D_i]C_{i,3}}
{\sum_i C_{i,3}}
\]

Despite being called “token-weighted,” the second is technically weighted by estimated all-T3 cost, which incorporates token estimates and assumed prices.

## 6. Reported classification metrics

- Exact agreement: \(P(T=D)\)
- Adjacent agreement: \(P(|T-D|\le1)\)
- Under-routed: \(P(T<D)\)
- Over-routed: \(P(T>D)\)
- Balanced accuracy: mean recall across D1, D2, D3
- D3 recall: fraction of D3 tasks sent to T3
- Spearman: rank correlation between router and evaluator scores

The default blend currently reports:

- 65.3% exact
- 97.1% adjacent
- 82.2% served
- 68.8% cost-weighted served
- 17.8% under-routed
- 45.5% estimated savings

The large gap between 82.2% task-served and 68.8% weighted-served means it disproportionately misses expensive/heavy tasks.

## 7. How the frontier is weighted

Every operating point is:

```text
x = policy cost / all-T3 cost
y = fraction of tasks served
```

Frontier AUC:

- Uses the upper envelope
- Integrates uniformly over cost shares from 25% to 100%
- Selects the winner using unweighted per-task served AUC

The headline benchmark winner reports:

- Frontier AUC: 0.892
- Served at 50% budget: 84.5%
- Cost needed for 90% served: 59.0%
- Weighted AUC: 0.690
- Weighted served at 50% budget: 54.5%

This exposes an important choice: the winner is selected by unweighted task AUC, not weighted AUC. Consequently, the λ router can favor many cheap tasks while neglecting large ones. The ordinal τ router actually has the better weighted AUC, 0.714.

## Important implementation caveat

The repo’s “default router” and “frontier winner” are not identical:

- Default pipeline: word+character TF-IDF ordinal model, blended 85/15 with the heuristic.
- Frontier winner: word TF-IDF reduced through 80-dimensional SVD, multiclass logistic regression, then λ dispatch.

The prose partially conflates them. For presentation purposes, they should be described as two separate policies: the balanced default and the tasks-per-dollar benchmark winner.
